judgements.why_changed: Initial assessment; changed is true as required.
judgements.reasons: Currently rung 3 ($300 billion to $350 billion in FY2027 full-year revenue). This is a cautious midpoint assessment in the absence of sufficient evidence, not a claim that the range has been established. The only listed evidence, e1, is management’s statement on FY2026 Q4 revenue and year-over-year growth, not an a fact of realized FY2027 full-year revenue or guidance. Nor can quarterly revenue annualized to $272 billion directly establish FY2027 full-year revenue. The dependent view v3’s rung 3 assessment of FY2027 data center revenue provides a neutral baseline; v1’s capex expectations and v7’s Rubin production ramp plan are only directional positives and are not sufficient to move to rung 1 or 2.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3, but disclosures added since the previous assessment show FY2026 full-year revenue of $215,938 million, up 65% year over year (e8). This is a relevant historical baseline fact, not merely the same statement with an additional source; therefore, a key figure supporting the assessment has changed. This new fact is not enough to change the FY2027 rung.
judgements.reasons: Rung 3 ($300 billion to $350 billion in FY2027 full-year revenue), a cautious midpoint assessment in the absence of direct facts or guidance on FY2027 total revenue; this is not an established revenue range. The FY2026 Q4 revenue and growth cited in e1 and the FY2026 full-year revenue and growth disclosed in e8 are historical performance that support a positive backdrop, but cannot determine which rung FY2027 full-year revenue will fall into. The dependent view v3’s rung 3 assessment of FY2027 data center revenue provides a neutral reference; v1’s capex expectations and v7’s Rubin production ramp plan remain directional inputs and cannot establish that FY2027 full-year revenue will reach a higher range.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3 compared with the previous assessment, but important new risk information has been incorporated: FY2026 revenue concentration among two direct customers, as well as management’s comments that China’s data center computing market is restricted and competitors’ ecosystems are expanding. These alter the risk evidence supporting the assessment, but do not move the conclusion to another rung.
judgements.reasons: Still rung 3 (FY2027 full-year total revenue of $300 billion to below $350 billion). This is a cautious midpoint assessment in the absence of an actual FY2027 total revenue result or direct guidance in the listed evidence, not an established revenue range. e1 and e8 show strong FY2026 growth and provide a positive backdrop, but do not directly determine the FY2027 total revenue range. e14 shows revenue concentration among two direct customers, increasing downside risk; e15 is management’s statement on restrictions in China and expanding competitor ecosystems, also pointing to downside, but neither can independently determine the revenue outcome. The dependent view v3 is a neutral reference, while v1’s capex expectations and v7’s Rubin production ramp plan provide directional positives; these inputs remain insufficient to support rung 1 or 2.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3, as in the previous assessment; the listed evidence and dependent views show no change in key facts or figures, so the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: Reassessment remains at rung 3 (FY2027 full-year total revenue of $300 billion or more but below $350 billion). e8 discloses FY2026 revenue of $215.938 billion, up 65% year over year, and e1 reports FY2026 Q4 revenue growth of 73% year over year. These provide a positive backdrop for continued FY2027 growth, but are neither an FY2027 total revenue result nor direct guidance. Customer concentration in e14 and the effects of restrictions in China and competitive ecosystems described in e15 are downside risks. e16 only confirms that the FY2027 compensation plan includes revenue thresholds, a baseline, and stretch targets; it does not disclose target amounts and cannot be used to infer a revenue range. The dependent view v3 is neutral; v1 and v7 provide directional positives, but neither is sufficient to move the assessment up a rung.

judgements.why_changed: The ladder remains at rung 3, but the addition of key revenue data—FY2027 Q1 revenue of $82 billion, up 85% year over year and 20% quarter over quarter—significantly strengthens the positive case. Under the rules, even without a rung change, a change in key figures supporting the assessment counts as a changed conclusion.
judgements.reasons: Still rung 3: the available evidence does not confirm FY2027 full-year total revenue or disclose revenue guidance that can directly determine the full-year range. e17 reports FY2027 Q1 revenue of $82 billion, up 85% year over year and 20% quarter over quarter, a strongly positive new signal; however, by evidence classification it is a party statement and cannot independently confirm full-year revenue of $350 billion or more. FY2026 full-year revenue was $215.938 billion (e8), and FY2026 Q4 revenue was $68 billion, up 73% year over year (e1); these provide growth context but do not determine the FY2027 full-year range. Customer concentration (e14) and restrictions on China’s data center computing market (e15) are downside risks; the compensation plan includes FY2027 revenue targets, but does not disclose their amounts (e16). The dependent view v3 is currently neutral and does not confirm that full-year data center revenue will reach a higher range; v1 and v7 provide a positive backdrop, but are insufficient to move the assessment to rung 2. The current assessment therefore remains at rung 3, or $300 billion to below $350 billion.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3, as in the previous assessment. The $81.6 billion in e27 is a more precise statement of the same quarterly figure, previously cited as Q1 revenue of about $82 billion, and does not constitute a change in key figures; e28’s Q1 data center revenue and growth drivers are already included in the dependent view v3. The new or repeated evidence strengthens the quarterly growth signal but does not change the full-year revenue range assessment.
judgements.reasons: Still rung 3. The available evidence does not provide an actual FY2027 full-year total revenue figure or revenue guidance sufficient to determine the full-year range directly. FY2027 Q1 total revenue was $81.6 billion, which annualizes to about $326.4 billion on a simple quarterly basis and falls within the rung 3 range; however, annualizing a single quarter is not a full-year result and cannot confirm full-year revenue of $350 billion or more. Q1 data center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year and driven by the Blackwell 300 ramp and demand for interconnect products, is clearly positive but remains quarterly data. FY2026 full-year revenue of $215.938 billion and Q4 revenue of $68 billion provide growth context; customer concentration and restrictions in China are downside risks. The FY2027 compensation plan includes revenue targets but does not disclose their amounts. The dependent view v3 remains neutral; v1’s capex expectations and v7’s Rubin shipment plans provide a positive backdrop, but are insufficient to move the full-year assessment to rung 2. Rung 3 therefore remains the best-supported current assessment, not an outcome confirmed by full-year facts.

judgements.why_changed: Moved from rung 3 to rung 2 since the previous assessment. FY2027 Q2 revenue guidance of $91 billion (excluding China data center computing revenue), combined with Q1 actual revenue of $81.6 billion and data center growth, makes FY2027 revenue above $350 billion better supported than before; however, there is still no full-year actual result or evidence sufficient to confirm $400 billion.
judgements.reasons: Rung 2 (FY2027 full-year total revenue of $350 billion to below $400 billion), the range best supported at present, though not yet confirmed by a full-year result. The key change is that FY2027 Q2 revenue guidance rose to $91 billion, plus or minus 2% (e41). Combined with Q1 actual revenue of $81.6 billion (e27), the first two quarters total about $172.6 billion; the second half would need about $177.4 billion, or an average of about $88.7 billion per quarter, to reach $350 billion. Q1 revenue was up 85% year over year and 20% quarter over quarter; data center revenue of $75.2 billion was driven by the Blackwell 300 ramp and interconnect demand (e27, e28), providing actual operating momentum toward this threshold. Revenue above $400 billion would require an average of about $113.7 billion in each of the second-half quarters; the available evidence is insufficient to make rung 1 the best-supported assessment. FY2026 full-year revenue of $215.938 billion and Q4 revenue of $68 billion are growth baselines (e8, e1), but do not directly determine the FY2027 full-year outcome. Risks include high customer concentration in FY2026 (e14), restrictions on the China market, and no Q1 shipments of data center Hopper products to China (e15, e30); however, the Q2 guidance explicitly excludes China data center computing revenue (e41). The dependent view v3 is now at rung 2, supporting a positive data center growth outlook but not constituting a total revenue forecast; v7’s Rubin production ramp plan provides a positive backdrop, not realized revenue; v1’s capex assessment provides only limited demand context.

judgements.why_changed: The rung remains 2, but e49 provides a new quantified fact: $119 billion in manufacturing, supply, and capacity commitments, of which $95 billion will be paid during the remainder of FY2027. This changes the factual basis supporting the assessment; the commitments are not revenue commitments, so they are insufficient to change the rung.
judgements.reasons: Rung 2 (FY2027 full-year total revenue of $350 billion to below $400 billion) remains the range best supported at present, but the full-year outcome is not confirmed. FY2027 Q1 actual revenue was $81.6 billion, and Q2 revenue guidance is $91 billion, plus or minus 2% . At the guidance midpoint, the first two quarters total about $172.6 billion; to reach $350 billion, the second-half quarters would need to average about $88.7 billion, while reaching $400 billion would require an average of about $113.7 billion. Q1 revenue grew 85% year over year; data center revenue was $75.2 billion, up 92% year over year and driven by the Blackwell 300 ramp and demand for interconnect products. Together with Q2 guidance, this supports a sustained high revenue run rate. However, these data do not confirm that the second half can reach the revenue level needed to support rung 1. The $95 billion in manufacturing, supply, and capacity commitments to be paid during the remainder of FY2027 support the view on supply scale, but are not revenue commitments. Restrictions on the China data center market, customer concentration, and infrastructure resource shortages are downside offsets. The dependent view v3 is at rung 2, providing a positive data center demand backdrop but not confirming full-year total revenue; v1 and v7 provide indirect positive context from capex and Rubin plans, respectively, but neither can substitute for actual total revenue evidence. Compared with the previous assessment, the ladder rung is unchanged; however, the new quantified operating fact of $119 billion in supply and capacity commitments, including $95 billion to be paid during the remainder of FY2027, changes the factual basis supporting the assessment, so changed is true.

judgements.why_changed: Initial assessment; marked as changed as required.
judgements.reasons: Placed in rung 3 ($250 billion to $300 billion) as a cautious midpoint judgment based on current evidence, not as a proven FY2027 revenue range. e2 is management's statement on FY2026 revenue and year-over-year growth, providing a strong historical growth base but no FY2027 revenue guidance. The 2026 capex assessment in view v1 remains a third-party expectation, while the Vera Rubin production timing in v7 remains a management plan. Both point in a bullish direction, but neither is evidence that FY2027 data center revenue has been achieved or directly confirmed. Therefore, this does not warrant moving up to rung 2 or rung 1, and there is insufficient bearish evidence to place it in rung 4 or rung 5.

judgements.why_changed: Unchanged from the previous assessment at rung 3. e9 provides an exact disclosure of FY2026 revenue, corroborating more precisely the same historical result described in e2 as approximately $194 billion, up 68% year over year. It is not new FY2027 guidance or a material change in key figures; therefore, the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: Placed in rung 3 (FY2027 data center revenue of $250 billion to $300 billion) as a cautious midpoint judgment in the absence of direct FY2027 revenue guidance, not as a proven revenue range. e9 confirms FY2026 data center revenue of $193.737 billion, up 68% year over year; e2 is management's description of the same historical result as approximately $194 billion. Strong historical growth provides a bullish backdrop, but cannot on its own confirm revenue above $250 billion in FY2027, much less $300 billion or $350 billion. The capex range in view v1 is a directional expectation, and the production shipments in v7 remain a management plan; both are bullish, but neither is evidence that FY2027 data center revenue has been achieved or directly confirmed.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3 versus the previous assessment. The supporting FY2026 revenue and year-over-year growth figures have not changed, and there is no new FY2027 revenue fact or direct guidance; repeated disclosure of the same historical result does not constitute a material factual change.
judgements.reasons: Reassessment remains at rung 3: the only existing direct facts confirm FY2026 data center revenue of $193.737 billion, up 68% year over year (described by management as approximately $194 billion), with no actual FY2027 data center revenue result or direct guidance. This cannot confirm FY2027 revenue above $250 billion, much less $300 billion or $350 billion. Historical growth provides a bullish backdrop; the capex expectation in view v1 and management's production-shipment plan in v7 are also bullish, but neither is sufficient to move the judgment to a higher revenue range.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 3 versus the previous assessment, but a key actual figure has been added: FY2027 Q1 data center revenue of $75 billion, with its simple annualized value reaching the $300 billion threshold. This is a material factual change; under the rules, the conclusion has changed.
judgements.reasons: Still placed in rung 3. China market restrictions and risks related to financing support are countervailing factors (e30, e50, e757). As of the evidence provided, there are no subsequent FY2027 quarterly actual data center revenue figures or full-year segment guidance.

judgements.why_changed: Initial assessment; marked as changed as required.
judgements.reasons: A third-party forecast puts 2026 capex “close to US$700 billion,” nearly US$120 billion higher than at the start of the year. This most strongly supports rung 3, or US$650 billion–US$700 billion. However, this is not actual capex that has occurred, so it cannot confirm that the range has been reached; the assessment remains directional.

judgements.why_changed: Still assessed at rung 3, unchanged from the previous assessment. The key support remains e6’s forecast of close to US$700 billion for 2026; e26 concerns 2027 and cannot replace or change this key evidence.
judgements.reasons: e6 says the 2026 capex forecast is close to US$700 billion, most strongly supporting rung 3, or US$650 billion–US$700 billion. However, this is an analyst forecast relayed by a third party, not actual capex that has occurred, so it cannot confirm that the range has been reached. e26 forecasts hyperscaler capex of more than US$1 trillion in 2027. Its year and scope are insufficient to determine which rung 2026 falls into; it is only a supplementary signal pointing in the high direction.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 3 versus the previous assessment, with no change to the key quantitative anchor, e6. e42 adds only a qualitative statement about accelerating activity and does not change the key figure underlying the range assessment; e26 remains a supplementary signal whose year and scope do not fully match.
judgements.reasons: The most relevant quantitative anchor remains e6: the analyst forecast is close to US$700 billion, closest to rung 3, but it is a third-party-reported forecast, not actual 2026 capex that has occurred, and cannot confirm that the rung has been reached. e26 concerns 2027 and hyperscalers, so it cannot directly determine which rung the combined 2026 capex of the five major cloud service providers and hyperscalers falls into. e42 is management’s statement that construction is accelerating, but it gives no figure that can be used to define the range. Therefore, rung 3 remains the best-supported assessment based on the available evidence, rather than a result confirmed by facts.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 3 versus the previous assessment; the new e67 is only a third-party view concerning investor concerns about returns and does not change the key facts or quantitative anchor supporting the assessment.
judgements.reasons: Rung 3 remains the best-supported assessment based on the available evidence, but is not a result confirmed by facts. e6’s 2026 forecast of close to US$700 billion is the most relevant quantitative anchor; it is an analyst forecast relayed by a third party and does not prove that actual capex falls within rung 3. e26 concerns 2027 and hyperscalers, so it cannot directly determine the 2026 total for this view; e42 says construction is accelerating but gives no quantified amount. e67 reflects investor concerns about AI returns, weakly pointing toward lower capex, but provides no fact of a capex cut or amount and is not enough to change the assessment.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 3, as in the previous assessment, with no change to the key anchor of e6’s 2026 quantitative forecast. The new e90 is only a conditional view, not a fact that capex has been cut, so it does not change the conclusion.
judgements.reasons: Rung 3 remains the best-supported assessment, but is not confirmed by actual capex facts. e6’s 2026 analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion is the most direct quantitative anchor and supports a level near rung 3; e26 concerns 2027 and cannot directly determine the 2026 amount. e42 says construction is accelerating but does not quantify capex. e67 expresses concern about returns on AI investment, while e90 is a conditional view that budgets could be cut if marginal returns decline. Neither provides a fact of a capex cut that has occurred, so neither is sufficient to move the assessment to a lower rung.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 3, with the key quantitative anchor remaining e6’s 2026 analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion; no new actual capex figure has changed this key evidence.
judgements.reasons: Rung 3 remains the best-supported assessment, but there is no evidence confirming which rung actual capex falls into. e6 is the most direct 2026 quantitative anchor: the analyst forecast is close to US$700 billion, supporting a level near rung 3. “Close to” does not explicitly mean reaching US$700 billion, so it is insufficient to assign rung 4. The other evidence mainly provides directional support or risks and cannot determine the actual 2026 amount: e26 concerns 2027, while e42 and e94 point to continued investment expansion; e67 expresses concerns about returns, and e90 is a risk of cuts conditional on declining marginal returns.

judgements.why_changed: Changed from rung 3 to rung 4 versus the previous assessment. The main reason is new e107, which explicitly forecasts 2026 spending at more than US$700 billion. This is a direct forecast change across the key threshold, but is still not a fact of actual spending.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 is currently the best-supported assessment, but no “a fact” confirms that actual 2026 capex has reached US$700 billion. The key change is e107: Reuters explicitly says 2026 spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion, directly moving the assessment above the rung 4 threshold; this is still a third-party forecast, not an actual spending result. e6’s analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, up nearly US$120 billion since the start of the year, supports a high level, but “close to” does not itself prove that US$700 billion has been reached. The other evidence provides directional context: e26 concerns 2027 and cannot directly determine the 2026 amount; e42 and e94 point to spending expansion, while e67 and e90 indicate concerns about returns and potential cut risks. Therefore, rung 4 is selected without claiming that facts have confirmed it.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4, as before; the evidence provided this time does not change the key figures or facts supporting the assessment, so the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 is currently the best-supported assessment: e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion, while e6 says the 2026 capex forecast for the five major cloud service providers and hyperscalers is close to US$700 billion and has risen nearly US$120 billion during the year. Together, they support a level around or above US$700 billion. However, these are third-party forecasts, and e107’s scope is not explicitly equivalent to the combined companies covered by this view. No “a fact” confirms the actual total, and there is no evidence limiting the amount to below US$750 billion or proving it has reached that level; therefore, rung 4 is the best-supported estimate, not a fact-confirmed result. Other evidence provides directional context: statements about accelerating construction and large spending point higher, while concerns about returns and potential budget contraction point lower; forecasts for 2027 cannot directly confirm the 2026 amount.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4, but new e127 gives a specific planned 2026 spending figure of approximately US$650 billion for four companies, while e126 says Alphabet raised its plan. These are important figures and plan information that change the evidence base supporting the current assessment. They do not move the conclusion to another rung, replace the prior figures, or confirm actual spending.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 is currently the best-supported assessment, but actual spending is not confirmed. e6 relays an analyst forecast that 2026 capex for the five major cloud service providers and hyperscalers will be close to US$700 billion; e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion, but its scope is not clearly equivalent to the companies covered by this view. e127 provides a more specific planned figure: four companies say their combined planned spending for 2026 is approximately US$650 billion. This is a plan, not actual spending, and excludes the fifth company. e126 says Alphabet raised its plan again but gives no amount. Taken together, this directional evidence most strongly supports the US$700 billion–US$750 billion range; there is insufficient basis to confirm the actual total or reliably establish that it has reached US$750 billion.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4 versus the previous assessment, with no material change to the key figures and facts supporting it. e152, like e126, says Alphabet raised its plan but provides no new amount; e153 adds an expectation of further spending increases, but gives neither an amount nor confirmation of actual spending. Therefore, these do not constitute a rung change or a change to a key figure.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported assessment, but there is still no evidence confirming the combined actual 2026 capex. e6 relays an analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, and e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion; the latter’s scope may not be equivalent to the combined companies covered by this view. In contrast, e127 reports planned spending of approximately US$650 billion for four companies, which is a plan rather than actual spending and excludes the fifth company. e126 and e152 both say Alphabet raised its 2026 capex plan but give no new amount; e153 only reports an expectation that three other companies will increase spending further. Overall, signals pointing to a high level continue to support rung 4, but are insufficient to confirm the actual total falls within this range or to support rung 5. No view input was relied upon.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4 versus the previous assessment; the key figures and facts supporting it have not changed: e6 remains an analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, e107 remains a broad forecast of more than US$700 billion in AI infrastructure spending, and e127 remains a plan of approximately US$650 billion for four companies. New or previously unelaborated directional evidence is insufficient to change the rung and does not constitute a change to a key fact or figure.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported assessment, but is not a confirmed actual result: there is no evidence that the combined actual 2026 capex of the relevant companies has fallen within a particular range. Directionally, e6 relays an analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, up nearly US$120 billion during the year, while e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion. The scope of both may not be equivalent to the companies covered by this view, so they can only push the assessment higher, not confirm rung 4. Conversely, e127 says four companies plan combined spending of approximately US$650 billion; this is a plan rather than actual spending and excludes the fifth company. e126 and e152 say Alphabet raised its plan but provide no amount, while e153 is only an expectation of increased spending by other companies. Taken together, these directional signals support rung 4 more than the other rungs, but uncertainty remains. No usable dependent view input.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4 versus the previous assessment; the listed evidence shows neither a total of actual capex that has occurred nor a replacement of the key guidance or figures supporting the assessment, so the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 is currently the best-supported assessment, but is not a confirmed actual result: there is no evidence that the relevant companies’ combined actual 2026 capex has fallen within any range. e6 relays an analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, up nearly US$120 billion during the year, and e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion; the scope of these forecasts may not be equivalent to the combined companies covered by this view. e127 says four companies plan combined spending of approximately US$650 billion; e123 says Microsoft plans to invest US$190 billion; e126 and e152 say Alphabet raised its plan; and e153 says investors expect other companies to increase spending. These are plans, reports, or expectations, not actual spending, but overall they support higher capex. Concerns about returns, sustainability, and spending levels (e67, e90, e121, e156) are downside signals; other positive statements or views provide directional support but cannot independently confirm the range. Overall, rung 4 is better supported than the other rungs, but uncertainty remains.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4 versus the previous assessment. The new directional views and reports strengthen either the case for high spending or the downside risks, but provide no new result for the relevant companies’ combined actual 2026 capex and do not change the key planned amounts or analyst forecast figures underpinning the previous assessment.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported assessment, but is not a confirmed actual result: there is no evidence that the relevant companies’ combined actual 2026 capex has fallen within a particular range. The more direct directional evidence is that e127 says four companies plan combined spending of approximately US$650 billion, e123 says Microsoft plans to invest US$190 billion, and e126 and e152 say Alphabet raised its plan. e6 says analysts expect close to US$700 billion, and e107 says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed US$700 billion. However, these plans, forecasts, and reports may not cover all companies or use the same scope as this view, and none can replace actual spending. Investor concerns about returns, sustainability, and financing structures (e67, e90, e121, e156, e181, e182) are downside signals; e144 is only a financing-negotiation rumour and makes no direct judgment on the spending range. Taken together, this directional evidence, which is not an actual result, supports rung 4 more than the other rungs, but certainty is limited.

judgements.why_changed: Still at rung 4 versus the previous assessment; current evidence shows no actual capex result and does not change the key figures supporting the assessment. New reports of Alphabet raising spending and Microsoft and Amazon not slowing spending are directionally consistent with existing signals of increases or sustained spending, and do not provide a new fact sufficient to change the rung or key figures.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported assessment, but is not a confirmed actual result: there is no evidence that the combined 2026 actual capex of the companies covered by this view has fallen within a particular range. Directional evidence includes e127’s report that four hyperscalers plan combined spending of approximately US$650 billion, e6’s analyst forecast of close to US$700 billion, and e107’s forecast of more than US$700 billion in 2026 AI infrastructure spending; multiple other items also report or expect continued spending increases. This supports rung 4 as more likely than rung 3, but the scope and coverage are not fully consistent, and forecasts, plans, and third-party reports cannot replace actual spending. There is insufficient basis to move up to rung 5 (US$750 billion or more); concerns about returns, sustainability, and financing structures are downside signals.

judgements.why_changed: The ladder remains at rung 4, but a key figure has changed: e192 gives Alphabet’s 2026 capex guidance as US$195 billion–US$205 billion, higher than the US$180 billion–US$190 billion previously reported in e193. Under the rules, a change to a key figure is marked as changed even if the rung does not change.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported view, but it is not a confirmed actual outcome: the available evidence does not provide total actual 2026 capex for the companies covered by this view. Directional support includes e127, which says four cloud providers had previously planned to spend about $650 billion; e6, which says analyst expectations for the five largest cloud service providers and hyperscalers were approaching $700 billion; and e107, which says 2026 AI infrastructure spending is expected to exceed $700 billion. New evidence e192 says Alphabet raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion. Compared with the prior guidance of $180 billion–$190 billion in e193, this further increases expected spending and supports a view above rung 3, at rung 4, but does not by itself prove that the total will reach $700 billion. e195 and e196 are a fact about cloud revenue and backlog, while e197 is management’s explanation of demand and higher spending. They help explain the increase but cannot replace evidence of total actual spending in 2026. Upside evidence remains insufficient to support rung 5. Concerns about returns, sustainability, and financing structure are downside signals, but are mainly views or risk assessments and do not prove that capex has already contracted.

judgements.why_changed: As last time, the view is rung 4. The additional Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222) is a relevant incremental fact, but it is neither full-year 2026 aggregate spending across the covered companies nor a change to the key guidance or forecast figures underpinning the previous view. It is therefore insufficient to change the conclusion.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported view, but it is not a confirmed full-year actual outcome: the available evidence does not provide aggregate 2026 capex for the companies covered by the question. Directionally, analyst expectations are approaching $700 billion (e6), and another report expects 2026 AI infrastructure spending to exceed $700 billion (e107). The approximately $650 billion in plans by four cloud providers (e127), together with Alphabet raising its 2026 guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), support a view that the total will fall in the $700 billion–$750 billion range. Alphabet cloud revenue, backlog, and management’s statements about demand (e195, e196, e197) provide context but cannot replace aggregate capex data. Microsoft’s reported quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222) is relevant actual spending information, but is insufficient to determine the full-year total. There is insufficient support for rung 5, which would require evidence that the total reaches $750 billion. Investor concerns about returns, spending sustainability, and financing structure (e67, e90, e121, e181, e182, e156) are downside risk signals but do not prove that spending has already contracted.

judgements.why_changed: As last time, the view is rung 4; there has been no change in the key expectations and guidance figures supporting it. New or listed information on actual quarterly spending is insufficient to change the full-year aggregate assessment, and no evidence has emerged that changes a key fact or figure.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported view, but it is not a confirmed full-year actual outcome: no a fact evidence provides aggregate 2026 capex for the companies covered by the question. The higher-spending view is mainly supported by analyst expectations approaching $700 billion (e6), reports expecting spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), plans of about $650 billion by four companies (e127), and Alphabet’s guidance increase to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192). These are expectations, reports, or management statements, not aggregate actual spending. Confirmable facts include Google Cloud revenue and backlog (e195, e196), as well as Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222); none is sufficient to determine the full-year total. The available evidence also does not support a total of $750 billion, so the view remains rung 4.

judgements.why_changed: After reassessing the available evidence, the view remains rung 4. The core figures and facts used in the previous conclusion—analyst expectations approaching $700 billion, planned spending of about $650 billion by four companies, Alphabet guidance of $195 billion–$205 billion, and Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion—have not been superseded or materially changed. Other evidence adds directional context but is insufficient to change the rung or key supporting figures.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported current view, but it has not been confirmed by actual results. No a fact in the available evidence provides aggregate 2026 capex for the companies covered by the question: Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222) is not a full-year total, and Google Cloud revenue and backlog (e195, e196) reflect demand, not total capex. The higher-spending view is mainly supported by analyst expectations approaching $700 billion (e6), reports expecting AI infrastructure spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), planned spending of about $650 billion by four companies (e127), and Alphabet raising its 2026 guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192). These figures are not fully comparable and are not aggregate actual spending; they support rung 4 but do not confirm $750 billion or more. Concerns about investment returns and spending sustainability (e67, e90, e121, e156) are countervailing signals, but none provides a fact of cuts that have already occurred.

judgements.why_changed: As last time, the view is rung 4; the cited evidence has not provided aggregate actual 2026 full-year capex within the scope of the question or changed the key figures underpinning the previous assessment. New signals mainly add support for the high-spending trend or reflect concerns that have not materialized as spending cuts, so they do not warrant a change of rung or a change in key facts.
judgements.reasons: The view remains rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), the best-supported range based on the weight of evidence, but not an outcome confirmed by actual full-year spending. Among directly confirmable facts, Microsoft quarterly capex was $41 billion (e222), while Google Cloud revenue and backlog were $24.8 billion and $514 billion, respectively (e195, e196); neither can independently establish the full-year 2026 aggregate capex of the companies in the question. The main support for the higher range is analyst expectations approaching $700 billion (e6), reports expecting AI infrastructure spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), planned aggregate spending of about $650 billion by four providers (e127), and Alphabet raising its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192). These are expectations, plans, or guidance, and their scopes are not fully equivalent to the actual full-year aggregate in the question; therefore, they do not support rung 5. Concerns about returns and spending sustainability (e67, e90, e121, e156) are countervailing downside signals, but provide no a fact of cuts that have occurred. Compared with last time, new or supplemental signals have not changed these key figures or the basis for the view, nor provided the full-year aggregate within the question’s scope.

judgements.why_changed: Compared with last time, the view remains rung 4, and the key supporting figures are unchanged: analyst expectations are still approaching $700 billion, the plans of four providers total about $650 billion, and Alphabet’s raised guidance is $195 billion–$205 billion. New or supplemental views have not provided aggregate full-year actual capex within the question’s scope or changed these key figures, so the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: The view remains rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), the range best supported by the available evidence, but not an outcome confirmed by actual full-year spending. Directly confirmable facts include Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222) and year-over-year growth in Alphabet cloud revenue, with backlog reaching $514 billion (e195, e196). These facts support strong investment demand but cannot independently establish aggregate 2026 full-year capex for the five largest cloud service providers and hyperscalers covered by the question. The main basis for the higher range remains analyst expectations approaching $700 billion (e6), reports expecting AI infrastructure spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), plans announced by four providers to spend about $650 billion in total (e127), and Alphabet raising its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192; prior guidance was $180 billion–$190 billion, e193). These expectations, plans, and guidance are not fully equivalent in scope to the actual full-year total asked about, and therefore do not support rung 5. Concerns about spending sustainability, returns, and overbuilding (e67, e90, e121, e156, e181, e182, e306) are countervailing downside signals but provide no a fact of overall spending cuts that have occurred.

judgements.why_changed: The view remains rung 4 compared with last time, and the key supporting figures and facts are also unchanged. Alphabet’s raised 2026 guidance and the superseded prior guidance, Microsoft’s quarterly capex, and Alphabet cloud business data were all included in the previous assessment. This time, no new fact confirms overall actual full-year spending or overall spending cuts.
judgements.reasons: The view remains rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), a range supported by the available evidence rather than a confirmed full-year actual total. Analyst expectations are approaching $700 billion (e6), reports expect AI infrastructure spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), and four providers had previously said they planned aggregate spending of about $650 billion (e127). Alphabet then raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), replacing prior guidance of $180 billion–$190 billion (e193). Microsoft quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222), together with growth in Alphabet’s cloud business and its backlog (e195, e196), is also consistent with spending remaining high. However, the scope and coverage of this evidence are not fully consistent, and it does not confirm the full-year actual total asked about; therefore, it does not support rung 5. Concerns about returns, sustainability, and overbuilding are downside signals but do not prove that overall spending cuts have occurred.

judgements.why_changed: The ladder remains at rung 4, but new evidence e322 gives an annual spending estimate of $750 billion, changing the key forecast figure at the upper end; e324 also estimates that spending by five companies could exceed $690 billion. Although these third-party estimates are insufficient to confirm the actual total or move the view to rung 5, the key forecast basis has changed from last time’s reliance on expectations of nearly $700 billion and above $700 billion.
judgements.reasons: The view remains rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), supported by the available evidence but not confirmed as the actual full-year total. Among a fact items, Microsoft reported quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222), and Alphabet cloud revenue and backlog were strong (e195, e196), but neither can independently determine the full-year total asked about. Alphabet’s 2026 guidance of $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), as stated by management, and the planned aggregate spending of about $650 billion by four providers (e127) are guidance and plans, not spending that has already occurred. Third-party estimates provide directional support: Reuters expects spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), FactSet estimates the combined total for five companies could exceed $690 billion (e324), and another estimate puts tech giant spending at $750 billion (e322). These forecasts and plans support rung 4, but their scopes, company coverage, and status as actuals versus forecasts differ, so they do not yet confirm rung 5. Downside concerns (such as e67, e90, e121, e156, e181, e182, e306) do not prove that overall capex has been reduced.

judgements.why_changed: The view remains rung 4 compared with last time, but Amazon’s disclosed 2026 cash capex expectation increased from about $200 billion to about $220 billion (e347), a key supporting figure change; under the rules, this counts as a change. Alphabet’s current guidance is also $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), above prior guidance of $180 billion–$190 billion (e193). The view has not changed to rung 5 because there is no full-year actual total within the question’s scope, and the scope and coverage of the $750 billion estimate are insufficient to confirm rung 5.
judgements.reasons: The view remains rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), the range with the strongest support from current evidence, not a confirmed full-year actual total. Upside support comes from several pieces of guidance and estimates: Alphabet raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192, versus $180 billion–$190 billion previously, e193); Amazon raised its 2026 cash capex expectation from about $200 billion to about $220 billion (e347); and four providers had previously announced plans totaling about $650 billion (e127). Among third-party estimates, Reuters expects relevant 2026 spending to exceed $700 billion (e107), FactSet estimates the combined spending of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle could exceed $690 billion (e324), and another estimate puts tech giant spending at $750 billion (e322). These figures support a total above $700 billion, but sources differ in scope, company coverage, and forecast status; in particular, e322 does not have a scope fully matching the question and cannot confirm a total of $750 billion. Available actuals also do not provide the full-year total asked about: Microsoft reported quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222), while Amazon disclosed net purchases of property and equipment of $169.07 billion over the past twelve months (e355). Neither is sufficient to determine the total for the five largest cloud service providers and hyperscalers for the full year. Therefore, the view does not move to rung 5.

judgements.why_changed: As last time, the view is rung 4. The previous assessment already incorporated Alphabet’s $195 billion–$205 billion guidance, Amazon’s expectation of about $220 billion, and the relevant third-party estimates. There is no new full-year actual total or evidence sufficient to change the key supporting figures.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the best-supported range estimate, but it is not a confirmed full-year actual total. The main evidence pointing to high spending is Alphabet raising its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), Amazon raising its cash capex outlook to about $220 billion (e347), and four vendors previously saying they planned to spend about $650 billion in total (e127). Third-party estimates include related spending exceeding $700 billion in 2026 (e107), a possible total of more than $690 billion for five companies (e324), and about $750 billion in spending by tech giants (e322); however, the definitions and company coverage are not fully consistent, so these estimates cannot confirm that spending reached rung 5. Actual quarterly or trailing-twelve-month data (e222, e355) also do not provide the full-year total asked for. In the absence of a full-year actual total covering the scope in question, the judgment remains at rung 4, the currently best-supported estimated range.

judgements.why_changed: Same as last time, rung 4, and the key inputs supporting this judgment have not changed: the planned and guided amounts shown in e127, e192, and e347 are the same as last time. New or supplemental estimates do not provide a full-year actual total within the scope of the question and are insufficient to confirm rung 5; therefore, the conclusion is unchanged.
judgements.reasons: Rung 4 remains the currently best-supported estimated range, but there is no full-year actual total for the scope in question to confirm this rung. Inputs supporting high spending include the four vendors’ previously stated plans to spend about $650 billion in total in 2026 (e127); Alphabet raising its 2026 guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192); and Amazon raising its cash capex outlook to about $220 billion (e347). FactSet estimates that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle could spend more than $690 billion in total (e324), while estimates of about $750 billion (e322) and claims of more than $700 billion (e107) support rung 5. However, the scope or definitions are not fully consistent, and these are third-party views, so they cannot confirm spending reached $750 billion. Microsoft’s quarterly capex of $41 billion (e222) and Amazon’s net purchases of property and equipment of $169.007 billion over the past twelve months (e355) also do not directly provide a full-year total. On balance, the judgment remains at rung 4.

judgements.why_changed: Same as last time, rung 4. The newly added figures for Microsoft’s quarterly capex and Amazon’s purchases over the past twelve months are useful actual spending data, but they do not constitute the 2026 full-year total for the scope in question, nor do they change the key annual guidance or estimates supporting the current range. The figures relevant to rung 5 remain third-party estimates whose definitions do not fully match.
judgements.reasons: The judgment remains at rung 4, the currently best-supported estimated range, rather than a range confirmed by a full-year actual total. Direct spending inputs remain elevated: the four vendors previously said they planned to spend about $650 billion in 2026 (e127); Alphabet raised its guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), and Amazon raised its 2026 cash capex outlook to about $220 billion (e347). Microsoft’s fourth-quarter capex of $41 billion and Amazon’s net purchases of property and equipment of $169.007 billion over the past twelve months reflect strong spending, but neither alone yields the 2026 full-year total for the companies within the target scope (e222, e355). Estimates supporting rung 5 include FactSet’s estimate that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle could spend more than $690 billion in total, along with broader estimates of about $750 billion and more than $700 billion (e324, e322, e107). However, these are third-party estimates, and their definitions do not fully match the scope of the question; they cannot confirm spending reached $750 billion. Rung 4 therefore remains the best-supported judgment.

judgements.reasons: The judgment remains at rung 4 ($700 billion–$750 billion), but this is a provisional assessment of the 2026 full-year total, not confirmation of an actual result. judgements.why_changed: Same as last time, still rung 4. judgements.reasons: Rung 4 is the currently best-supported range judgment, not a confirmed full-year actual total. Key evidence of high spending includes the four cloud providers’ earlier statement that they planned to spend about $650 billion in total in 2026 (e127); Alphabet raising its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion–$205 billion (e192), and Amazon raising its cash capex outlook to about $220 billion (e347); FactSet’s estimate that the five companies could spend more than $690 billion in total (e324); a forward-looking signal that Big Tech spending will exceed $730 billion in total (e622); and an estimate that the four largest hyperscalers will spend nearly $745 billion (e691). This evidence supports spending reaching $700 billion, but there is no full-year actual total sufficient to confirm it reached $750 billion. In particular, e691 remains a third-party estimate, not a full-year result that has occurred. e222 and e355 are actual spending for a quarter or rolling period and cannot directly replace the 2026 full-year total asked for.

judgements.why_changed: Still rung 4, as in the previous assessment. judgements.reasons: The judgment is rung 4, the currently best-supported full-year range assessment; it does not mean that the full-year actual total has been confirmed. judgements.why_changed: Changed from rung 4 last time to rung 5. The latest evidence updates the consensus forecast for 2026 capex by the five largest hyperscalers to nearly $800 billion (e816), above rung 5’s $750 billion threshold; the earlier forecast of about $733 billion for five companies (e765) and estimate of nearly $745 billion (e691) no longer represent the latest key forecast level.
judgements.reasons: The best-supported full-year range view has been raised to rung 5: the latest analyst consensus says capex by the five major hyperscalers in 2026 is “close to $800 billion” (e816), above the $750 billion threshold; a related Goldman Sachs forecast also puts 2026 AI infrastructure investment by the five major hyperscalers at about $800 billion (e814). The previous forecast of about $733 billion for the five companies (e765) and estimate of close to $745 billion for the four largest hyperscalers (e691) were close to, but below, the rung 5 threshold. Alphabet and Amazon raised their 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion to $205 billion (e192) and about $220 billion (e347), respectively, providing company-level support for the high-spending view. Importantly, rung 5 remains the most strongly supported forecast, not an outcome confirmed by actual full-year 2026 spending; the main evidence for crossing the $750 billion threshold remains analyst and third-party forecasts.

judgements.reasons: NVIDIA said the FY2027 full-year GAAP tax rate is expected to be 17.0% to 19.0% , consistent with rung 3's range and the description “within the company's stated outlook range.” This evidence is a company statement, not a realized full-year tax rate; the conclusion is therefore based on the company's outlook and does not mean the actual rate has been determined.

This range spans rung 2 and rung 3; using the guidance midpoint of 17% as the point estimate, rung 3 applies because its range includes 17% , and 17% –18% falls within the company's stated outlook range. This determination is based on the company's outlook and does not mean the actual full-year tax rate has been determined. judgements.why_changed: The ladder remains at rung 3, but the company guidance underpinning the determination changed from 17% –19% to 16% –18% , with both endpoints changing; under the rules, the conclusion has therefore changed.

views.question: Will the comprehensive cooperation signed by NVIDIA and SK Group be formally implemented by December 31, 2026, and cover AI factory construction and AI memory supply?

judgements.why_changed: Initial assessment; recorded as changed as required.
judgements.reasons: To date, the overall collaboration is still described as a plan, and the parties signed a “letter of intent to formally finalize the agreement”; this is insufficient to prove that the overall collaboration has been formally finalized. Although a long-term AI memory partnership between SK hynix and NVIDIA has been established, and NVIDIA says the parties will jointly develop next-generation AI memory, the available evidence does not prove that AI factory construction has also been formally finalized. The two conditions for rung 1 are therefore not currently met. Since the deadline has not yet arrived, this is only a current assessment based on available evidence and does not establish that the collaboration will still be unfinalized as of 2026-12-31.

They move the assessment toward rung 1, but do not independently prove that the overall collaboration covering both items has been formally finalized. The current assessment is therefore rung 2; 2026-12-31 has not yet arrived, so this is not an assertion about the outcome on that date.
